title: Modified Family-Vicsek Scaling and Probability Distributions for Brownian Castle Interfaces
authors: Noah Sublett, Charles Sutton, Benjamin Long, Daniel B. Dougherty
abstract: The Brownian Castle is a new interface growth model that is a variation on the well-known ballistic deposition model that results in an entirely new universality class. We present numerical verification that the interface width for BC interfaces displays modified Family-Vicsek scaling properties up to finite size corrections. Specifically, we find a growth exponent of $β=0.470 \pm 0.012$ and a roughness exponent of $α=1.01 \pm 0.018$. The scaling is modified at short times with a size scaling exponent that described the early time dependence of interface width on length. The probability distribution of heights for the BC interface shows significant deviations from simple Gaussian behavior and the probability distribution of height changes shows a Cauchy-Lorentz form consistent with expectations for a process involving relatively large jumps.
summary: This paper investigates the Brownian Castle (BC) interface growth model, finding it belongs to a new universality class distinct from standard models like Ballistic Deposition. Through extensive simulations, the authors determine specific scaling exponents and show that the height fluctuations follow non-Gaussian statistics characterized by Cauchy-Lorentz tails. This work advances the understanding of complex, driven interfaces in statistical physics.
main_problem: The study characterizes a new universality class associated with interface growth dynamics by analyzing modified Family-Vicsek scaling properties and probability distributions.
main_result: The Brownian Castle (BC) interface exhibits modified scaling exponents ($ eta \approx 0.47$, $\alpha \approx 1.01$) and shows that the height change distribution follows a Cauchy-Lorentz form, suggesting large jumps.
method: Numerical simulations are used to extract growth and roughness exponents via fitting double logarithmic plots, complemented by data collapse analysis and statistical testing of probability distributions.
model_or_system: The system is the Brownian Castle (BC) interface growth model, a variation on Ballistic Deposition that allows for material removal. It is compared against established models like BD, which falls into the KPZ universality class.
key_observables: Interface width $w(L, t)$, growth exponent ($ eta$), roughness exponent ($\alpha$), and probability distributions of height changes ($p(dh)$).
important_parameters: System size ($L$) up to 512 sites, time steps up to $10^6$, and the derived scaling exponents $ eta=0.47 \pm 0.01$ and $\alpha=1.01 \pm 0.01$.
main_assumptions: The standard scaling relationship $z = \alpha/ eta$ may break down due to finite size effects, which is noted when comparing derived exponents to the exponent observed during data collapse ($z=3$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic growth rules for BD vs. BC, show interface width evolution over time and system size (determining $ eta$ and $\alpha$), and demonstrate near-perfect data collapse using a specific scaling function.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the BC model variation, presents numerical simulations to calculate scaling exponents ($\alpha,  eta$) via fitting, analyzes data collapse for consistency checks, and finally examines probability distributions (heights and height changes) to characterize the underlying stochastic process.
why_interesting: While focused on classical interface growth, the analysis of non-Gaussian statistics (Cauchy-Lorentz tails) and deviations from standard scaling laws provides insights into complex, non-equilibrium dynamics relevant to open quantum systems or driven many-body processes where simple thermal assumptions fail.
